message.content:
I don’t have direct access to your network, so I can’t tell you the exact speed right now. But you can quickly find out by running a speed test yourself. Here are a few easy ways to do it:

---

## 1. **Use an Online Speed Test**

| Browser | How to |
|---------|--------|
| Chrome / Edge / Firefox | Go to <https://www.speedtest.net> or <https://fast.com> and click “Go” (or “Start Test”). |
| Safari | Same as above – just open the URL and hit “Go.” |

These sites will measure your **download** and **upload** speeds (in Mbps) and give you a ping (latency) value.

---

## 2. **Command‑Line Speed Test (Windows)**

If you prefer the terminal, you can use the free `speedtest-cli` tool.  
1. **Install Python** (if you don’t already have it).  
2. Open PowerShell or Command Prompt and run:

```powershell
pip install speedtest-cli
```

3. Then run:

```powershell
speedtest
```

You’ll see output like:

```
Testing from Your ISP (Your City)...
Retrieving speedtest.net configuration...
Testing download speed........................................
Testing upload speed..........................................
Download:  85.23 Mbit/s
Upload:    12.45 Mbit/s
Ping:      24.7 ms
```

---

## 3. **Built‑in Windows Tool (Optional)**

Windows 10/11 has a built‑in “Network Speed Test” in the Settings app:

1. Open **Settings** → **Network & Internet** → **Status**.  
2. Click **Network speed test** (if available).  
3. It will launch a web‑based test similar to Speedtest.net.

---

## 4. **Mobile Apps**

If you’re on a phone, the same sites work in the mobile browser, or you can download the official Speedtest app from the App Store / Google Play.

---

### Quick Tips

- **Run the test at different times** (morning, afternoon, evening) to see how traffic affects speed.  
- **Connect via Ethernet** (wired) if possible; Wi‑Fi can introduce variability.  
- **Restart your router** if you notice consistently low speeds.

---

Let me know if you’d like help interpreting the results or troubleshooting slow speeds!
